items.new_information: 以暴露度×迁移摩擦评估各链量子就绪度

evidence.quote: Let me explain this post-quantum migration map measuring quantum exposure X migration friction, and why it plays such an important role in the assessments for quantum-readiness.
When we talk about quantum readiness, we need to pay attention to 2 equally important factors:
1. Quantum exposure, meaning how vulnerable a chain is to an attack from a quantum computer
2. Migration friction, meaning how difficult and challenging is it going to be for end users and apps to upgrade to post-quantum security.

Some protocols will need at least a soft fork (hello Bitcoin) to reach quantum-safety, some will require users to navigate their way through clunky UX, and in some cases, users will only need a quick approval for an upgrade.

evidence.quote: In July, a week after @Revolut announced it would delist $USDT for EEA clients, I published a chart with a record: $855M of weekly USDT volume on Revolut wallets. The number travelled, it was cited, and it looked logical - users taking their money out before it gets taken out for them. Two months later I recomputed the same series: the same week came out at

Once I separated them, it turned out that on the peak week of 13 July roughly $780M moved between Revolut's own addresses - mostly between the hot wallet and a settlement wallet, in near-equal amounts in both directions.

This loop was not created by the delisting: it was already running at $220 - 330M a week in mid-June, and during the delisting it simply peaked. Client USDT transfers that week, across all chains, were about $76M.

The rule I take from this: for a custodial player, volume is not published until it is split into client, internal, and LP settlement. Internal is cut by address list. Settlement is cut by counterparties with mirrored flows. What remains is what deserves to be called volume.
